prompt: What is job analysis?

options.text: The process of collecting, analysing and setting out information about jobs
Practices carried out to identify and attract potential employees
Application of techniques to select and appoint a competent person
The rationale for HR planning and selection decision making

explanation: Job analysis collects and sets out information about the job (→ job description and person specification). Identifying and attracting candidates is recruitment; applying techniques to appoint a competent person is selection.

prompt: What is selection?

options.text: The process of collecting, analysing and setting out information about jobs
Practices carried out to identify and attract potential employees
Application of techniques to select and appoint a competent person
The rationale for HR planning and selection decision making

explanation: Selection applies techniques to choose the right candidate out of the pool. Attracting the pool is recruitment – good recruitment makes selection possible.

prompt: The video describes two parallel activities at the start of recruitment: job analysis and person-organisation fit. Which question does P-O fit answer?

options.text: What kind of attitudes and behaviours are essential to succeed here?
How much does the job pay compared with the market?
Which recruitment agency should we use?

explanation: Job analysis: what does the job involve (can the person do the job?). P-O fit: will the person fit and succeed in this organisation?

prompt: Which item belongs in the PERSON SPECIFICATION rather than the job description?
explanation: The job description describes the job (title, location, reporting lines, purpose, tasks, conditions); the person specification describes the ideal person (education, experience, skills, attitudes).

prompt: Which item does NOT belong in the JOB DESCRIPTION?
explanation: Attitudes belong to the person specification.

prompt: In a person specification, which of the following is a “disqualifying factor”?

options.text: Lack of an essential licence or accreditation
A candidate has less experience than desirable

explanation: Disqualifying factors rule a candidate out, e.g. a missing essential accreditation. “Less than desirable” is a nice-to-have, not a knock-out.

prompt: What does the distinction “essential vs desirable characteristics” in a person specification mean?
explanation: Essential = the candidate must have it; desirable = it is an advantage but not required.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the video's points on person-organisation fit?

options.text: Firm and people analyses rather than job analysis

explanation: The four points: organisational philosophy, competencies, firm and people analyses, and the critique of “cloning” (reduced diversity).

prompt: Which of these is a BEHAVIOURAL (rather than technical) competency?
explanation: Behavioural competencies describe how people work (teamwork, initiative, customer focus); technical ones are specialist skills.

topic: P-O fit – firm and people analyses
prompt: When are “firm and people analyses rather than job analysis” particularly useful?

options.text: When jobs change quickly and one fixed job description would soon be outdated
When the firm hires only for routine jobs
When the firm wants to minimise recruitment costs
When the law requires a job description

explanation: Looking at what the whole firm needs and what kind of people succeed there helps when jobs are fluid.

prompt: Which of the following is not a CLOSED type of recruitment method?
explanation: The company's website is an open (public) search, like adverts, other websites and social networks. Closed: word of mouth, links with schools/colleges/universities, recruitment agencies.

prompt: What is the main drawback of closed searches such as referrals?

options.text: The pool is small and candidates resemble current staff – less diversity
They attract too many unsuitable applications
They are illegal in the EU

explanation: Closed searches are cheap, fast and pre-filtered, but the pool is small and reproduces the current workforce (social capital, in-group favouritism).

prompt: What is the main drawback of open searches such as job boards and newspaper adverts?

options.text: Many unsuitable applications have to be screened, which costs time and money
Candidates are pre-filtered by the agency

explanation: Open searches give a large, more diverse pool – but more screening and cost (CIPD: 58 % saw more applications).

prompt: Which of the following is a RECRUITMENT method rather than one of the selection methods listed in the video?
explanation: Adverts attract candidates (recruitment). The video's selection methods: self-selection, application forms, CV, references, interviews, assessment centres, tests, probationary periods, innovative methods.

prompt: What does “self-selection” mean as a selection method?

options.text: Candidates drop out themselves after getting a realistic picture of the job
The candidate rates his or her own performance

explanation: A realistic job preview lets unsuitable candidates opt out themselves – cheap and effective.

prompt: A selection method “accurately measures what it is supposed to measure”. Which criterion is this?
explanation: Validity: a good score on the method predicts good job performance.

prompt: Two interviewers assess the same candidate with the same method and reach very different scores. Which criterion is violated?
explanation: Reliability = consistency: same method, same result – whoever applies it and whenever.

prompt: A retailer considers a two-day assessment centre for 5,000 store assistants. Which criterion is most at risk?
explanation: Practicability: acceptable to all parties and cost-effective. An assessment centre may be valid but is far too costly at this volume.

prompt: According to Universum, what is the employer brand?

options.text: The distinctive attributes and qualities of an organisation as an employer
What makes the organisation the employer of choice for a desired target group
The logo and colours used in job adverts

explanation: Universum → value proposition for employees; CIPD → distinctive attributes and qualities (reputation as an employer).

prompt: Which statement about employer branding is NOT in the video?

options.text: There is a global need for talent and a highly competitive labour market
A strong employer brand brings about twice as many applications
Online employer information is easy to find but not always accurate
A strong employer brand removes the need for selection methods

explanation: If the firm does not shape its brand, others do (Glassdoor, LinkedIn, Facebook reviews). It supports attraction – selection is still needed.

prompt: The video says employer branding helps to “manage the psychological contract through the brand”. What does this mean?

options.text: The brand sets employees' unwritten expectations before they join – and the promise must then be kept
The brand replaces the written employment contract
The brand allows the firm to lower pay
The brand obliges employees to stay for a minimum period

explanation: The brand creates expectations; if the employment experience does not match, the psychological contract is broken.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three reasons in the video's “why is it relevant?” slide?

options.text: Manage the psychological contract through the brand
Make the brand a source of common identity for employees

explanation: The three reasons: psychological contract, signalling values and prestige, common identity → commitment.

prompt: According to the Inditex feedback, recruitment activities must balance the organisation's and the candidate's needs. What is the tension?

options.text: Informing (a realistic picture) vs attracting (selling the job)

explanation: Recruitment must both inform candidates realistically and attract them.

prompt: Which option does the Inditex feedback explicitly ask you to consider in a recruitment strategy?
explanation: “Consider the possibility of internal recruitment”: known performers, motivation and lower cost.

prompt: Which check is NOT part of the Inditex feedback on proposing selection methods?

options.text: Which aspect of performance in the job description does each method measure?
How do the methods work together to increase validity and reliability?
Are all relevant requirements of the job description evaluated?
Which method does the hiring manager personally prefer?

explanation: The feedback asks what each method measures, how the methods work together, whether repetitions are necessary and cost-effective, and whether all requirements are covered – not personal preferences.

prompt: The two Inditex positions are in the same firm but in different countries. Why does this matter for the recommendation?

options.text: It does not matter – the same strategy must be used everywhere
Labour markets, channels and culture differ, so the recruitment and selection strategy should be adapted to the context
Only the salary needs to be adjusted
Different countries require different job descriptions by law

explanation: The task explicitly asks you to consider the context, P-O fit, validity/reliability/practicability and cost-effectiveness.

prompt: What does the CIPD (2026) report show about the number of applications?

options.text: More applications led to equally more suitable candidates
58 % of employers saw more applications, but only 33 % saw more suitable candidates
Suitable candidates rose faster than applications

explanation: More applications ≠ better hires – a key argument for targeted recruitment.

basis.ref: CIPD Resourcing and Talent Planning Report 2026

prompt: Which attraction method did employers rate as most effective in the CIPD (2026) report?
explanation: Own corporate website (40 %), generic job boards (35 %), internal advertising (32 %), consultants (29 %), professional networks (28 %), referrals and organic content (24 % each).

basis.ref: CIPD Resourcing and Talent Planning Report 2026

prompt: What was the median cost per hire for senior managers/directors in the CIPD (2026) report?
explanation: £3,500 for senior managers/directors and £2,000 for other employees (technology, advertising, agency fees, tests, onboarding).

basis.ref: CIPD Resourcing and Talent Planning Report 2026

prompt: For which roles did employers report the greatest difficulty attracting candidates (CIPD, 2026)?
explanation: 53 % had difficulties, mainly for senior and skilled roles (18 % also for low-skilled).

basis.ref: CIPD Resourcing and Talent Planning Report 2026
